claim: TPL2 is expressed in both innate and adaptive immune cells in the peripheral immune system to regulate inflammatory responses.
source: TPL2 is expressed in both innate and adaptive immune cells in the peripheral immune system to regulate inflammatory responses (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2018

claim: TPL2 expression is enriched in brain myeloid cells and endothelial cells in human and mouse cortex.
source: RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis of FACS-purified cells from human (Srinivasan et al., 2020) and mouse (Zhang et al., 2014) cortex revealed that TPL2 expression is enriched in brain myeloid cells and endothelial cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from cited studies and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: TPL2 expression was highly induced in bulk brain tissue and sorted microglia following LPS injection in mice.
source: In an acute neuroinflammation study, in which mice received intraperitoneal injection of the endotoxin lipopolysaccharide (LPS), TPL2 expression was highly induced in both bulk brain tissue (GSE196401) and sorted microglia (Srinivasan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from GSE196401 and cited study

claim: TPL2 gene expression was upregulated in bulk tissue and sorted microglia from the P301S tauopathy mouse model.
source: We also found that TPL2 gene expression was upregulated in bulk tissue (GSE186414) and sorted microglia from the P301S tauopathy mouse model (Friedman et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from GSE186414 and cited study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: TPL2 protein levels in the cortex of Alzheimer's disease patients showed an increase compared to healthy control brains.
source: Western blot analysis of TPL2 protein levels in the cortex of Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients showed an increase compared to healthy control brains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: LPS stimulation dramatically increased phosphorylation of ERK and p38 in mouse primary microglia cultures.
source: Upon LPS stimulation, phosphorylation of ERK and p38 was dramatically increased, and this increased phosphorylation was significantly dampened in the presence of the TPL2 small molecule inhibitors G-767 and G-432 (Figure 1A and B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: TPL2 inhibitors significantly dampened LPS-induced phosphorylation of ERK and p38 in microglia.
source: Upon LPS stimulation, phosphorylation of ERK and p38 was dramatically increased, and this increased phosphorylation was significantly dampened in the presence of the TPL2 small molecule inhibitors G-767 and G-432 (Figure 1A and B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: LPS-induced NF-κB pathway activation was not affected by TPL2 inhibition in microglia.
source: In contrast, as expected, LPS-induced nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway activation, as measured by elevation of phospho-p65, was not affected by TPL2 inhibition.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing no change in phospho-p65 with TPL2 inhibition

claim: TPL2 inhibitors did not affect baseline phosphorylation of ERK, p38 or p65 without stimulation in microglia.
source: Of note, the TPL2 inhibitors did not affect baseline phosphorylation of ERK, p38 or p65 without stimulation (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: TPL2 mediates MAPK signaling but not NF-κB signaling in microglia.
source: These results are consistent with TPL2 mediating mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling, but not NF-κB signaling, in microglia.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of TPL2 inhibition on MAPK vs NF-κB pathways

claim: TPL2 plays an important role in regulating cytokine production by myeloid cells in the peripheral immune system via the MAPK signaling pathway.
source: It is well established that TPL2 plays an important role in regulating cytokine production by myeloid cells in the peripheral immune system via the MAPK signaling pathway (Arthur and Ley, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arthur and Ley, 2013

claim: LPS-induced production of inflammatory cytokines TNFα, IL-1α, IL-6, and CXCL1 was greatly reduced in the presence of TPL2 inhibitors in microglia.
source: Consistently, using multiplex immunoassays to measure cytokine release by microglia, we found that LPS-induced production of inflammatory cytokines, such as TNFα, IL-1α, IL-6, and CXCL1, was greatly reduced in the presence of TPL2 inhibitors (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by multiplex immunoassay data shown in Figure 1C and supplements

claim: Microglia cultured from TPL2-KD mice showed dramatically decreased LPS-induced cytokine production.
source: Moreover, when we analyzed cytokine release by microglia cultured from TPL2-KD mice, there was dramatically decreased LPS-induced cytokine production (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by multiplex immunoassay data shown in Figure 1D and supplement

claim: TPL2 is a key regulator of the microglial MAPK signaling pathway and proinflammatory cytokine responses.
source: Overall, this data indicates that TPL2 is a key regulator of the microglial MAPK signaling pathway and proinflammatory cytokine responses, and thus could play an important role in modulating neuroinflammation in the brain.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on MAPK signaling and cytokine production

claim: Activated microglia can be neurotoxic by releasing factors such as proinflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species.
source: Activated microglia can be neurotoxic by releasing factors such as proinflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species (Glass et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glass et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2015

claim: Stimulation of microglia and neuron co-cultures with LPS + IFNγ resulted in almost complete neuronal loss.
source: Stimulation of microglia and neuron co-cultures with LPS + interferon gamma (IFNγ), a stimulus reported to induce strong microglia activation (Straccia et al., 2011), resulted in almost complete neuronal loss as measured by MAP2 immunostaining (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by MAP2 immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: TPL2 inhibitor G-767 nearly fully rescued neuronal loss induced by LPS + IFNγ stimulation in microglia-neuron co-cultures.
source: Strikingly, when the TPL2 inhibitor G-767 was added to the co-culture, the neuronal loss induced by the LPS + IFNγ stimulation was nearly fully rescued.
evidence: Supported by MAP2 immunostaining data showing rescue of neuronal loss

claim: Co-culturing WT neurons with microglia from TPL2-KD mice rescued stimulation-induced neuronal loss.
source: In addition, when WT neurons were co-cultured with microglia isolated from TPL2-KD mice, stimulation-induced neuronal loss was also rescued (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by MAP2 immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: LPS + IFNγ stimulation can induce dramatic increases of iNOS expression in microglia and subsequent release of nitric oxide, which is neurotoxic.
source: Several groups have shown that LPS + IFNγ stimulation can induce dramatic increases of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) expression in microglia and subsequent release of nitric oxide (NO), which is neurotoxic (Papageorgiou et al., 2016; Sheng et al., 2011; Straccia et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Papageorgiou et al., 2016; Sheng et al., 2011; Straccia et al., 2011

claim: LPS + IFNγ stimulation increased iNOS protein levels in primary microglia cultures over time.
source: Consistent with this mechanism, we found that when primary microglia cultures were stimulated with LPS + IFNγ, iNOS protein levels were increased and accumulated over time (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: TPL2 small molecule inhibition significantly reduced iNOS protein in stimulated microglia by 50%.
source: TPL2 small molecule inhibition significantly reduced iNOS protein in stimulated microglia (50% reduction) and stimulated microglia isolated from TPL2-KD mice also showed a dramatic reduction of iNOS (85% reduction) (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C-E

claim: Stimulated microglia isolated from TPL2-KD mice showed an 85% reduction of iNOS.
source: TPL2 small molecule inhibition significantly reduced iNOS protein in stimulated microglia (50% reduction) and stimulated microglia isolated from TPL2-KD mice also showed a dramatic reduction of iNOS (85% reduction) (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C-E

claim: Treatment with iNOS inhibitor 1400W almost fully rescued neuronal loss in microglia-neuron co-cultures.
source: Treatment with the iNOS inhibitor almost fully rescued the neuronal loss (Figure 2F, G), indicating that NO production by activated microglia is a key contributor to neuronal death in this co-culture system.
evidence: Supported by MAP2 immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F and G

claim: NO production by activated microglia is a key contributor to neuronal death in the microglia-neuron co-culture system.
source: Treatment with the iNOS inhibitor almost fully rescued the neuronal loss (Figure 2F, G), indicating that NO production by activated microglia is a key contributor to neuronal death in this co-culture system.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of neuronal loss by iNOS inhibition

claim: LPS induced significantly increased expression of disease-associated microglia (DAM) genes in WT mice.
source: Using previously defined CNS myeloid gene modules (Friedman et al., 2018), we found that LPS induced significantly increased expression of disease-associated microglia (DAM) genes (e.g. Il1r1, Axl) in WT mice, whereas this microglia activation response was attenuated in LPS-treated TPL2-KD mice (Figure 3A, D, and E).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A, D, and E

claim: The microglia activation response to LPS was attenuated in TPL2-KD mice.
source: Using previously defined CNS myeloid gene modules (Friedman et al., 2018), we found that LPS induced significantly increased expression of disease-associated microglia (DAM) genes (e.g. Il1r1, Axl) in WT mice, whereas this microglia activation response was attenuated in LPS-treated TPL2-KD mice (Figure 3A, D, and E).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A, D, and E

claim: Homeostatic microglia gene expression was downregulated by LPS in WT mice but relatively unchanged in LPS-treated TPL2-KD mice.
source: Homeostatic microglia gene expression (e.g. Tmem119, Cx3cr1) was downregulated by LPS in WT mice, but relatively unchanged in LPS-treated TPL2-KD mice (Figure 3C, D, and E), consistent with TPL2-KD microglia being in a less activated state after stimulation.
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C, D, and E

claim: TPL2-KD microglia are in a less activated state after LPS stimulation compared to WT microglia.
source: Homeostatic microglia gene expression (e.g. Tmem119, Cx3cr1) was downregulated by LPS in WT mice, but relatively unchanged in LPS-treated TPL2-KD mice (Figure 3C, D, and E), consistent with TPL2-KD microglia being in a less activated state after stimulation.
evidence: Inferred from the preservation of homeostatic gene expression in TPL2-KD mice

claim: LPS-induced increase in microglia proliferation genes in WT mice was normalized in TPL2-KD mice.
source: Interestingly, an increase in microglia proliferation genes by LPS in WT mice was also normalized in TPL2-KD mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3E

claim: LPS-induced activated astrocyte gene expression was attenuated in TPL2-KD mice.
source: Consistent with a reduction of microglia activation of astrocytes, LPS-induced activated astrocyte gene expression (e.g. Cd44, Srgn) was also attenuated in TPL2-KD mice (Figure 3B, D, and E).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B, D, and E

claim: Several cytokines elevated in LPS-treated WT mouse brains had significantly lower levels in TPL2-KD mouse brains.
source: In parallel to the RNA-seq measurements, we also measured brain cytokine levels and found that several cytokines such as IL-1α, IL-6, and CXCL1 that were elevated in LPS-treated WT mouse brains had significantly lower levels in TPL2-KD mouse brains (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by multiplex immunoassay data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Cytokines released by microglia in response to LPS stimulation can induce the transition of astrocytes from a resting state to an activated/reactive state that can be neurotoxic.
source: In addition to directly affecting neurons, microglia have also been shown to indirectly cause neurotoxicity by activating astrocytes. Cytokines released by microglia in response to LPS stimulation can induce the transition of astrocytes from a resting state to an activated/reactive state that can be neurotoxic (Liddelow et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liddelow et al., 2017

claim: Only a restricted set of cytokines exhibited TPL2 dependence in cultured astrocytes compared to microglia.
source: In contrast to the broader TPL2 dependence of cytokine release by cultured microglia (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), only a much more restricted set of cytokines exhibited TPL2 dependence in cultured astrocytes.
evidence: Supported by comparison of cytokine data from microglia and astrocyte cultures

claim: TPL2-dependent activated astrocyte genes identified in vivo exhibited much less TPL2-dependent activation in cultured astrocytes.
source: Moreover, TPL2-dependent activated astrocyte genes identified in the in vivo LPS study (Figure 3B) exhibited much less TPL2-dependent activation in cultured astrocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of in vivo and in vitro gene expression data

claim: TPL2-dependent astrocyte activation observed in vivo following LPS injection was probably largely contributed to indirectly via the function of TPL2 in microglia.
source: These results suggest that the TPL2-dependent astrocyte activation we observed in vivo following LPS injection was probably largely contributed to indirectly via the function of TPL2 in microglia, but there was also potentially some contribution of cell-autonomous function of TPL2 in astrocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the differential TPL2 dependence in vivo vs in vitro

claim: TPL2 plays a key role in microglia and astrocyte activation in vivo.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that TPL2 plays a key role in microglia and astrocyte activation in vivo, and show that acute neuroinflammation can be reduced by ablation of TPL2 kinase activation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined in vivo data on microglia and astrocyte activation

claim: Acute neuroinflammation can be reduced by ablation of TPL2 kinase activation.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that TPL2 plays a key role in microglia and astrocyte activation in vivo, and show that acute neuroinflammation can be reduced by ablation of TPL2 kinase activation.
evidence: Supported by the combined data showing reduced inflammation in TPL2-KD mice

claim: TPL2-KD mice showed moderate reduction of microgliosis after optic nerve crush but no rescue of retinal ganglion cell loss.
source: However, although we observed moderate reduction of microgliosis in TPL2-KD mice after ONC, we did not see rescue of retinal ganglion cell loss (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A

claim: TPL2-KD rats showed significantly reduced microgliosis after tMCAO but no beneficial effects on body weight loss, behavioral deficits, or lesion volume.
source: Similarly, despite significantly reduced microgliosis, we did not see beneficial effects in TPL2-KD rats in terms of body weight loss, behavioral deficits, and lesion volume measured by MRI after tMCAO (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–H).
evidence: Supported by MRI, behavioral, and immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-H

claim: Reduced neuroinflammation with TPL2-KD may not be sufficient for neuroprotection in cases of severe acute tissue damage.
source: These results highlight that reduced neuroinflammation with TPL2-KD may not be sufficient for neuroprotection in cases of severe acute tissue damage.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of neuroprotection in ONC and tMCAO models despite reduced inflammation

claim: TauP301S transgenic mice overexpress human mutant Tau and develop pathology marked by phosphoTau accumulation, neuroinflammation, and brain atrophy as the mice age, especially in the hippocampus.
source: These transgenic mice overexpress human mutant Tau and develop pathology marked by phosphoTau accumulation, neuroinflammation, and brain atrophy as the mice age, especially in the hippocampus (Wu et al., 2019; Yoshiyama et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2019 and Yoshiyama et al., 2007

claim: TPL2-KD did not affect the % area of the brain covered by Iba1 or GFAP in non-transgenic mice.
source: TPL2-KD did not affect the % area of the brain covered by Iba1 or GFAP in non-transgenic mice.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data

claim: In TauP301S mice, Iba1 and GFAP signals were greatly increased reflecting gliosis, and TPL2 kinase deficiency slightly ameliorated this gliosis.
source: In TauP301S mice, the Iba1 and GFAP signals were greatly increased reflecting gliosis, and TPL2 kinase deficiency slightly ameliorated this gliosis (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: Phospho-Tau pathology was somewhat reduced in TauP301S;TPL2-KD mice.
source: Interestingly, phospho-Tau pathology (measured by AT8 staining) was also somewhat reduced in TauP301S;TPL2-KD mice (Figure 4A, B), potentially reflecting the interplay between neuroinflammation and Tau pathology (Didonna, 2020; Maphis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by AT8 immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: The levels of several cytokines and chemokines that were significantly increased in TauP301S mouse brains were blunted in TauP301S;TPL2-KD brains, including CXCL9, CXCL10, IL6, and IFNγ.
source: Consistent with the gliosis changes, the levels of several cytokines and chemokines that were significantly increased in TauP301S mouse brains were blunted in TauP301S;TPL2-KD brains, including CXCL9, CXCL10, IL6, and IFNγ (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by multiplex immunoassay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: P301S mice showed increases in relative abundance of microglia, T-cells, and mixed immune cells.
source: P301S mice showed increases in relative abundance of several cell types, including microglia, T-cells, and a cluster we initially labeled as 'mixed immune cells' (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq cellularity analysis shown in Figure 5 and supplements

claim: The mixed immune cells cluster contained a unique cell type corresponding to dendritic cells.
source: Further analysis of the mixed immune cells cluster showed that it contained a unique cell type with expression of distinct genes compared to microglia or T-cells (e.g. Plbd1, Mgl2, Clec9a) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A). Subclustering of the mixed immune cells identified this unique cell type as a distinct cluster from microglia or T-cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), and mapping onto ImmGen cell type data (Heng and Painter, 2008) revealed this population corresponded to dendritic cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq analysis and ImmGen mapping shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: Dendritic cells showed an elevation in P301S brains.
source: Like microglia and T-cells, dendritic cells also showed an elevation in P301S brains (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 4, C21).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq cellularity analysis shown in Figure 5C and supplement

claim: TPL2-KD did not have a significant effect on the proportion of most cell types in non-transgenic mice.
source: Strikingly, while TPL2-KD did not have a significant effect on the proportion of any of the 13 cell types in non-transgenic mice, and did not alter the proportion of most cell types in P301S brains, TPL2-KD significantly reduced the abundance of T-cells and dendritic cells in P301S brains (Figure 5B and C; Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq cellularity analysis shown in Figure 5B, C and supplement

claim: TPL2-KD significantly reduced the abundance of T-cells and dendritic cells in P301S brains.
source: Strikingly, while TPL2-KD did not have a significant effect on the proportion of any of the 13 cell types in non-transgenic mice, and did not alter the proportion of most cell types in P301S brains, TPL2-KD significantly reduced the abundance of T-cells and dendritic cells in P301S brains (Figure 5B and C; Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq cellularity analysis shown in Figure 5B, C and supplement

claim: P301S;TPL2-KD mice have reduced infiltration of peripheral immune cells compared to P301S mice.
source: This indicates that P301S;TPL2-KD mice have reduced infiltration of peripheral immune cells compared to P301S mice.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced abundance of T-cells and dendritic cells

claim: T-cell number in the fimbria area was increased in TauP301S mouse brains, and the increase was normalized by TPL2-KD.
source: To corroborate the scRNA-seq results, we also performed T-cell immunohistochemistry (IHC) using fixed brain tissue sections. T-cell number in the fimbria area (the area that has the most robust T-cell abundance in previous studies of TauPS2APP mice; Lee et al., 2021b) was increased in TauP301S mouse brains, and the increase was normalized by TPL2-KD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C

claim: T-cells are present in the brains of human AD patients and preclinical disease models.
source: Given the presence of T-cells in the brains of human AD patients and preclinical disease models, and the beneficial effects of T-cell depletion in mouse disease or injury models (Chen et al., 2023; Gate et al., 2020; Laurent et al., 2017; Merlini et al., 2018; Togo et al., 2002), the decreased presence of peripheral immune cells in TauP301SxTPL2-KD mouse brains could have beneficial effects.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: T-cell depletion has beneficial effects in mouse disease or injury models.
source: Given the presence of T-cells in the brains of human AD patients and preclinical disease models, and the beneficial effects of T-cell depletion in mouse disease or injury models (Chen et al., 2023; Gate et al., 2020; Laurent et al., 2017; Merlini et al., 2018; Togo et al., 2002), the decreased presence of peripheral immune cells in TauP301SxTPL2-KD mouse brains could have beneficial effects.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2023; Gate et al., 2020; Laurent et al., 2017; Merlini et al., 2018; Togo et al., 2002

claim: The decreased presence of peripheral immune cells in TauP301SxTPL2-KD mouse brains could have beneficial effects.
source: Given the presence of T-cells in the brains of human AD patients and preclinical disease models, and the beneficial effects of T-cell depletion in mouse disease or injury models (Chen et al., 2023; Gate et al., 2020; Laurent et al., 2017; Merlini et al., 2018; Togo et al., 2002), the decreased presence of peripheral immune cells in TauP301SxTPL2-KD mouse brains could have beneficial effects.
evidence: Speculative inference based on cited studies

claim: Both CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell numbers were increased in P301S brains, and TPL2-KD significantly reduced the abundance of both cell types.
source: Cellularity analysis showed that both CD4+ and CD8+ cell numbers were increased in P301S brains, and TPL2-KD significantly reduced the abundance of both cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq cellularity analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5C

claim: CD8.4, the largest T-cell subcluster, was decreased in P301S;TPL2-KD mouse brains.
source: When the relative abundance was compared within the T-cell population, CD8.4, the largest T-cell subcluster, was decreased in P301S;TPL2-KD mouse brains (Figure 5—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq cellularity analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5D

claim: CD8.4 cells expressed marker genes of exhausted T-cells, such as Nr4a2 and Pdcd1.
source: CD8.4 cells expressed some marker genes of exhausted T-cells, such as Nr4a2 and Pdcd1, which are usually induced by chronic/persistent exposure to antigens and/or inflammation (Odagiu et al., 2020; Wherry, 2011; Wherry and Kurachi, 2015; Yi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq gene expression data and citations

claim: Within the TauP301S group, when comparing TPL2-KD to TPL2-WT mice, differentially expressed genes were only detected in microglia.
source: However, within the TauP301S group, when comparing TPL2-KD to TPL2-WT mice, DEGs were only detected in microglia (Figure 6A), consistent with TPL2 being most highly expressed by microglia in the mouse brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by pseudo-bulk differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: The most upregulated genes in P301S microglia were consistently upregulated to a lesser extent in P301S;TPL2-KD microglia, including cytokines like Tnf and multiple immediate early genes such as Egr1.
source: Analysis of the protein-coding DEGs showed that the most upregulated genes in P301S microglia were consistently upregulated to a lesser extent in P301S;TPL2-KD microglia, including cytokines like Tnf and multiple immediate early genes (IEGs) such as Egr1 (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: A subcluster of microglia (C11) expressing high levels of IEGs was elevated in P301S mice, and this elevation was ameliorated by TPL2-KD.
source: On the other hand, a subcluster of microglia (C11) expressing high levels of IEGs (e.g. Fos, Egr1-3, Atf3) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) was elevated in P301S mice, and this elevation was ameliorated by TPL2-KD (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq cellularity analysis shown in Figure 6E and supplement

claim: IEG expression was upregulated in astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, OPCs, and VSMCs in P301S mice, but the upregulation was only normalized by TPL2-KD in microglia.
source: Calculation of IEG gene set score for every defined cell type (pseudo-bulk) showed IEG expression was up in astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, OPCs, and VSMCs, but the upregulation was only normalized by TPL2-KD in microglia (and to some extent in VSMCs, although not statistically significant, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by gene set score analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G

claim: IEG expression can be regulated by MAPK signaling pathways and TPL2 is a key regulator of MAPK signaling.
source: As IEG expression can be regulated by MAPK signaling pathways and TPL2 is a key regulator of MAPK signaling (Bahrami and Drabløs, 2016; O'Donnell et al., 2012), these results are consistent with a specific role for TPL2 in TauP301S microglia.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bahrami and Drabløs, 2016 and O'Donnell et al., 2012

claim: A subcluster of microglia (C20) that was elevated in P301S and normalized by TPL2-KD expressed high levels of MHC class II genes.
source: Another subcluster of microglia (C20) that was elevated in P301S and normalized by TPL2-KD in the P301S mice expressed high levels of MHC (major histocompatibility complex) class II genes (e.g. Cd74, H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, etc.), which are usually expressed by antigen presenting cells and are important for the generation of immune responses via interaction with T-cells (Neefjes et al., 2011; Roche and Furuta, 2015; Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6F and supplement, and citations

claim: The reduction of P301S MHCII expressing microglia by TPL2-KD combined with the reduction of infiltrating T-cells and dendritic cells points to a normalization of adaptive immune function in P301S brains.
source: The reduction of P301S MHCII expressing microglia by TPL2-KD in P301S mice combined with the reduction of infiltrating T-cells and dendritic cells points to a normalization of adaptive immune function in P301S brains.
evidence: Inferred from the combined changes in MHCII microglia, T-cells, and dendritic cells

claim: Microglia-mediated synapse elimination has been observed in AD mouse models including P301S mice.
source: As microglia-mediated synapse elimination has been observed in AD mouse models including P301S mice (Hansen et al., 2018; Stephan et al., 2012; Wilton et al., 2019), we quantified synapse density by measuring spine number in sparsely labeled dendrites using GFP expression driven by the Thy1-GFP-M transgene.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2018; Stephan et al., 2012; Wilton et al., 2019

claim: P301S;TPL2-KD mice had significantly increased spine density compared to P301S mice.
source: Spine analysis by ex vivo imaging found that P301S;TPL2-KD mice had significantly increased spine density compared to P301S mice (Figure 7A), consistent with potentially reduced microglia removal of spines in P301S;TPL2-KD mice.
evidence: Supported by ex vivo imaging data shown in Figure 7A

claim: TauP301S mice develop neurodegeneration, including ventricle enlargement and brain volume reduction, that can be measured by volumetric MRI.
source: Previous studies have shown that TauP301S mice develop neurodegeneration, including ventricle enlargement and brain volume reduction, that can be measured by volumetric MRI (vMRI) (Dejanovic et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dejanovic et al., 2018 and Wu et al., 2019

claim: In WT mice, ventricle volumes stayed stable and neocortex and whole brain volumes increased between 6 and 9 months.
source: In WT mice, ventricle volumes stayed stable and neocortex and whole brain volumes increased between 6 and 9 months, and TPL2 kinase deficiency did not alter the trajectory of the brain volume changes.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal vMRI data

claim: TPL2 kinase deficiency did not alter the trajectory of brain volume changes in WT mice.
source: In WT mice, ventricle volumes stayed stable and neocortex and whole brain volumes increased between 6 and 9 months, and TPL2 kinase deficiency did not alter the trajectory of the brain volume changes.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal vMRI data

claim: P301S mice developed brain atrophy, as indicated by increasing ventricle volumes and decreasing brain volumes between 6 and 9 months.
source: As expected, P301S mice developed brain atrophy, as indicated by increasing ventricle volumes and decreasing brain volumes between 6 and 9 months.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal vMRI data

claim: TPL2-KD significantly ameliorated the ventricle enlargement and brain volume decline in TauP301S mice.
source: Strikingly, TPL2-KD significantly ameliorated the ventricle enlargement and brain volume decline in TauP301S mice (Figure 7B, C), indicating a robust neuroprotective effect of inhibition of TPL2 kinase activity in this mouse model.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal vMRI data shown in Figure 7B and C

claim: Inhibition of TPL2 kinase activity has a robust neuroprotective effect in the TauP301S mouse model.
source: Strikingly, TPL2-KD significantly ameliorated the ventricle enlargement and brain volume decline in TauP301S mice (Figure 7B, C), indicating a robust neuroprotective effect of inhibition of TPL2 kinase activity in this mouse model.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of brain volume loss

claim: Plasma NfL was strongly increased in P301S mice, but TPL2-KD did not significantly affect NfL levels.
source: However, while plasma NfL was strongly increased in P301S mice, TPL2-KD did not significantly affect NfL levels (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by plasma NfL measurements shown in Figure 7D

claim: While plasma NfL increases in P301S mice, neuroprotection can be achieved irrespective of NfL levels.
source: This indicates that while plasma NfL increases in P301S mice, neuroprotection can be achieved irrespective of NfL levels.
evidence: Inferred from the dissociation between NfL levels and neuroprotection

claim: TauP301S mice displayed behavioral hyperactivity as indicated by significantly increased total beam breaks, ambulatory bouts, and rearing behavior compared with WT mice.
source: As previously seen (Dejanovic et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019), compared with WT mice, 9-month-old TauP301S mice displayed behavioral hyperactivity as indicated by significantly increased total beam breaks, ambulatory bouts, and rearing behavior.
evidence: Supported by open field test data and citations

claim: TPL2 kinase activity deficiency did not impact the locomotor activity of non-transgenic mice, but prevented the hyperactivity in the tauopathy mice.
source: TPL2 kinase activity deficiency did not impact the locomotor activity of non-transgenic mice, but prevented the hyperactivity in the tauopathy mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by open field test data shown in Figure 7E

claim: P301S mice had somewhat elevated baseline freezing behavior and failed to exhibit an increase in freezing behavior in response to the auditory stimulus in trace fear conditioning test.

claim: The beneficial effects in the TauP301S mice indicate that modulating immune cell function via eliminating TPL2 kinase activity can be beneficial in a context with chronic neuroinflammation where neurodegeneration gradually occurs over time.

claim: The tauopathy model study reveals multiple aspects of pathophysiology that are normalized by TPL2-KD concordant with rescue of neurodegeneration and behavior.

claim: A recent study found T-cell depletion resulted in a robust reduction of neurodegeneration and behavioral deficits in TauP301S mice.

evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2023

claim: The reduced amount of T-cells in the brains could be particularly relevant to the protective effects of eliminating TPL2 kinase activity.

claim: A recent study found that endothelial TPL2 regulates blood-brain barrier permeability and immune cell infiltration in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model.

claim: Conditional KO of TPL2 in endothelial cells but not microglia, astrocytes, or neurons, protected against EAE disease severity.

evidence: Supported by reference to findings from Nanou et al., 2021

claim: The endothelial cluster 7 data is consistent with TPL2-dependent regulation of the MAPK signaling pathway in endothelial cells in TauP301S mice.

claim: TPL2 is expressed in both innate and adaptive immune cells in the peripheral system.

claim: Microglia orchestrate both protective and damaging responses during neurodegeneration in conditions such as AD.
